evidence.reference_title: The first case of antenatal presentation in COG8-congenital disorder of glycosylation with a novel splice site mutation and an extended phenotype.
evidence.snippet: We present the first case of antenatally diagnosed COG8-CDG with facial dysmorphism and additional features such as Dandy-Walker malformation and arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, thus expanding the phenotype of this rare disorder.

nodes.description: Disease-causing COG8 alleles are truncating: a splice-site change in intron 3 plus a two-nucleotide deletion removing the last 47 residues, a homozygous nonsense variant removing the 76 C-terminal residues, two frameshift variants, and a homozygous variant creating a new splice site in exon 5. Every reported lesion removes part of the COG8 C-terminus.

nodes.description: Loss of the Cog1-Cog8 bridge between lobe A and lobe B leaves only smaller COG subcomplexes. Patient fibroblasts lack COG8 protein entirely and show reduced levels or mislocalisation of several other COG subunits, with Cog1 absent from the Golgi; acute COG8 knockdown in HeLa cells reproduces the loss of Cog1.

evidence.reference_title: Further delineation of COG8-CDG: A case with novel compound heterozygous mutations diagnosed by targeted exome sequencing.
evidence.snippet: Targeted exome sequencing was performed to screen all CDG type II-related genes, and two novel frameshift mutations were found: c.171dupG (p.Leu58Alafs*29) and c.1656dupC (p.Ala553Argfs*15) in COG8.

nodes.description: Acute shRNA depletion of COG8 in HeLa cells, used alongside patient fibroblasts to separate acute from chronic consequences of COG8 loss. Golgi organisation is disrupted, cisternae dilate, untethered vesicles accumulate, and Cog1 falls by roughly 80%.

Fibroblasts from the index patient lack COG8 protein, mislocalise other COG subunits, are deficient in N- and O-glycan sialylation and show a slowed brefeldin A response. Re-expression of normal COG8 corrects all three, which is the rescue experiment that establishes COG8 loss as sufficient to cause the cellular phenotype.

nodes.description: Cerebellar involvement is a recurring theme across the congenital disorders of glycosylation; in COG8-CDG it is documented by brain MRI in one patient.

nodes.description: COG8-CDG produces a type II CDG biochemical pattern. The defect is specifically terminal: the first sialic acid is added normally to otherwise largely normal N-glycans, but subsequent sialylation fails, and both N- and O-glycans are affected. Severity of the sialylation deficiency differs between reported patients.

nodes.description: Because glycosylation modifies a large fraction of the secreted and membrane proteome, the hyposialylation defect degrades many unrelated client glycoproteins at once. In COG8-CDG the resulting disease is predominantly neurological with hepatic, growth, skeletal and, in the antenatally ascertained case, structural brain involvement.

nodes.description: Beyond N- and O-glycosylation, glycosaminoglycan modification of proteoglycans is reduced when any COG subunit is missing. COG8 is one of the two lobe-bridging subunits for which the reduction is least marked, and COG8-deficient cells retain normal glycosaminoglycan chain lengths on secreted proteoglycans, unlike cells lacking COG2-COG7. This is a knock-out cell-line result; proteoglycan synthesis has not been reported in COG8-CDG patient material.
